card.profile: Formation dance is a style of ballroom dancing performed by teams of couples arranged in formations. It involves synchronized choreography where couples execute patterns such as diamonds, circles, and lines. Routines last about six minutes and combine individual couple technique with coordinated team movements. Formation dancing is practiced internationally in both Latin and Standard ballroom styles, often in competition.
card.insight: Formation dancing began in 1932 at London's Astoria Ballroom, evolving into a competitive sport with teams of 6-8 couples performing synchronized routines judged on patterns and synchronicity.

card.profile_long: Formation dance originated in 1932 at the Astoria Ballroom in London, introduced by Olive Ripman under the name "pattern dancing." It quickly became a competitive dance form, with contests beginning in England in the 1930s and spreading worldwide. Teams typically consist of 6 to 8 couples who perform choreographed routines that combine individual dancesport techniques with coordinated group patterns. These patterns, also called shapes or images, include diamonds, squares, diagonals, circles, and lines, and the clarity and transitions of these shapes are key judging criteria. The choreography may be based on a single dance or a medley of dances, with Latin formation including Cha Cha, Rumba, Jive, Paso Doble, and Samba, and Standard formation including Waltz, Quickstep, Tango, Viennese Waltz, and Foxtrot. Routines last up to six minutes, including walk-on and walk-off sections often featuring free-form choreography and lifts, which are prohibited during the judged segment. Synchronization and timing to the music's beat are critical, with judges marking teams on synchronicity and execution. Formation dance is governed internationally by the International DanceSport Federation (IDSF), with competitions such as the British National Championships at the Blackpool Dance Festival and the Donaupokal Invitational in Vienna. In German-speaking countries, formation teams follow similar rules under the Deutscher Tanzsportverband (DTV) and World DanceSport Federation (WDSF), with music structured into an entrance, main part, and exit, separated by gong signals. Music themes vary widely, often arranged from known pieces to suit the dance character. Special figures unique to formation dancing include roundabouts, chain reactions, and the Velberter Rose, which add visual impact. Men's attire in Standard formation is traditionally black or midnight blue tailcoats, while Latin formation allows more color but requires uniformity. Formation dancing remains a living tradition with active international competition and evolving choreography.

sections.origins_and_history: Formation dancing began in 1932 at London's Astoria Ballroom, introduced by Olive Ripman as "pattern dancing." It became a competitive sport in England during the 1930s and expanded internationally. The dance form was featured on BBC's Come Dancing program in the 1960s and has grown globally since.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Teams of 6 to 8 couples dance choreographed routines lasting up to six minutes, including walk-on and walk-off sections. Couples perform synchronized steps to the beat, forming patterns such as diamonds, circles, and lines. Latin formation includes Cha Cha, Rumba, Jive, Paso Doble, and Samba, while Standard formation includes Waltz, Quickstep, Tango, Viennese Waltz, and Foxtrot. Solo work is limited in Standard but common in Latin. Lifts are allowed only in walk-on/off sections. Technique involves precise timing, spatial awareness, and coordinated transitions between patterns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for formation dance is arranged to fit the choreography, typically lasting six minutes with entrance, main, and exit parts separated by a gong. The main part, which is judged, lasts 3 to 4.5 minutes. Music themes vary widely and may be orchestral or edited recordings. The rhythm matches the dance style, with Latin and Standard styles each having characteristic tempos and meters. Instruments are not specifically described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men in Standard formation wear black or midnight blue tailcoats; in Latin formation, men wear uniform colored shirts, often black. Women may wear varied dresses within competition rules. The dance floor is used fully to display patterns, with clear visibility of formations prioritized. Walk-on and walk-off sections allow more freedom in costume and choreography.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Formation dance is performed in competitions governed by the International DanceSport Federation and national bodies. It is a sport emphasizing teamwork, synchronization, and technical skill. The dance is also performed for exhibitions and television programs. Judging focuses on synchronicity, pattern clarity, and execution.
sections.notable_figures: Olive Ripman introduced formation dancing in 1932. Specialist choreographers include Ona Skaistutė Idzelevičienė, Roberto Albanese, Horst Beer, and Rachael Holland.
sections.regional_variants: Formation dancing is practiced internationally with notable competitions in England, Germany, and Austria. German-speaking countries have structured leagues under the Deutscher Tanzsportverband, emphasizing Standard and Latin formations. Variants exist in other dance styles like Bhangra and jazz, but the ballroom formation style is distinct.
sections.lineage: Formation dance evolved from ballroom dancing and pattern dancing introduced in early 20th-century England. It developed alongside individual dancesport competitions and incorporated elements from jazz and ballet in walk-on/off sections.

basic_steps: Couples line up in formation (e.g., diamond or line)
Start synchronized basic steps of chosen dance (e.g., Cha Cha basic step)
Execute coordinated turns or chain reactions on beat
Transition smoothly to next formation pattern
Walk off formation in coordinated exit

teaching.formation: Teams of 6-8 couples arranged in geometric patterns such as diamonds, circles, lines, or squares
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic steps and simple formations; advanced dancers perform complex patterns and solo sections

Teams consist of 6 to 8 couples performing synchronized choreography.
Routines last up to six minutes including walk-on and walk-off sections.
Formation choreography includes patterns like diamonds, squares, circles, and lines.
Music is arranged with entrance, main judged section, and exit separated by a gong.
Lifts are allowed only in walk-on and walk-off sections, not during judged routine.
Men in Standard formation wear black or midnight blue tailcoats; Latin men wear uniform colored shirts.
Formation dance is governed internationally by the International DanceSport Federation (IDSF).
